entry.title: Earthlings
entry.content:
The first 5 chapters of Earthlings are pretty innocent compared to the final (6th) chapter.

Sure there is some sexual, and physical, violence, but its all like... understandable.

The main character is weird in a personable way that makes some valid points. We've all had points in our lives where we felt like everybody was out to get us, we couldn't fit in, etc etc. This character has that turned up to 11, but you still can at least empathize with her. When life gets you down it's easy to escape the pain with some fantastical stories like "I'm actually an alien so it makes sense that nobody understands me."

Where this diverges is in the final chapter, which I think is why this was in Man Carrying Thing's "10 scary books" video because it is truly fucked up. Not the most fucked up book I've ever read, but certainly it makes the list.

I don't want to get into too much detail, because I still think the book is worth reading. The final chapter is almost a... release. A lot of pent up energy from the rest of the book, finally coming to it's extreme yet obvious conclusion.

Is it a fun read? Yeah, it's a weird book and weird books are fun.

Would I suggest everybody read it? No, but if you self identify as a weird book reader, you should check it out.

entry.title: There Is No Antimemetics Division
entry.content:
I've been following SCP off and on trough the last few years. I'm a fan of Control and Alan Wake and those feel like an extension of the SCP universe.

Having followed this space unfortunately some of these stories were already spoiled either by YouTube videos or reading the "there is no Antimemetics Divison" webseries -- which I don't recall reading at any point but some of these stories were definitely already in my brain... maybe it's a memetic implanting memories in my consciousness... or I am just forgetful...

SCP is a fun world to read about since it's basically just X-Files but even less structure.

There is not Antimemetics Division does do a good job of breaking out of the SCP mold in a few ways:

  • A theme of Alzheimer's, while not in text but I got that vibe at least.
  • A theme of societal memory loss, people in general forgetting atrocities that were horrible.
  • A pretty authentic-to-the-narrative love story.

The Alzheimer's one was the most impactful to me. I've wanted to write a story about mental decay, memory loss, not being able to trust your own senses, that sort of thing, and while it doesn't go that far it does explore some of the themes, so I had interest there.

While not in the text directly, characters struggle to know what's real, what they used to know, and often lose friends and family and loved ones because of an Antimemetic monster taking their memories without them even knowing, or remembering.

Finally, I liked how as a story construction this was able to introduce an unknowingly untrustworthy narrator, because they keep forgetting things that happened -- that you even read in previous chapters!

It also plays with what information the characters have in a fun way that you can usually only get with like... flashbacks. In most stories once a character learns a piece of information they know it forever, but in this the author was able to do some interesting, and not too cheap, selective memory tricks to produce interesting situations.

This is all just what I liked about the story, and honestly reading it back I could see if you might be turned off by this description. I promise it's a fun sci-fi romp with interesting story telling and fun ideas you don't read much of.

entry.title: Call Me a Cab
entry.content:
Call Me a Cab was a suggestion by Man Carrying Thing (YouTube) and I thoroughly enjoyed it.

Of the books that Man Carrying Thing recommends I can't say for certain why this book was the first one I actually cracked open, but I can speculate. First, I've wanted to get into crime novels and this is labeled as such on every website about it -- ironically there is no crime (at least not in a meaningful way like you would expect from the "Crime Novel" genre. Second, the cover is very pulp-novel coded, which is interesting for a novel released in 2022! Finally, it's got a pretty lady on the front in a striking pose, I won't deny that sex sells.

Anyway I'm really glad I did start reading this! It was written in the 70s and only just now published posthumously, so it's a period piece? (Is it a period piece if it's set in modern day... when it was written?)

I also really like road-trip novels. I also enjoyed I'm Starting to Worry About This Black Box of Doom which is also a road-trip novel -- almost identical actually:

Woman calls a local taxi/uber ride driven by mediocre nobody Woman then decides/reveals she needs a ride across the country

Both books also, ultimately at least, have very low stakes. Call me a Cab is just about a woman deciding if she wants to marry her boyfriend and needing more time to think and make her decision.

Along the way you get these little vignettes. The weird anxious guy at the Motel whose bed won't stop vibrating, the couple who need to get to the ER to deliver their baby, a one-night stand with a bartender. These little stories make it a 50/50 split between a fast-friends story and a collection of short stories.

I also think road trip novels show you what makes the country so wonderful. Yeah, our politicians are garbage, our policies are backward, it's hard to survive, but we've got good people and a diversity of them.

This quote keeps going around, usually attributed to "some european visiting for the world cup":

if you want to hate America, watch the news. If you want to love America, drive across it

And I think that sums it up pretty well.

entry.title: Murderbot diaries
entry.content:
All Systems Red (2017)

I had a thoroughly good time reading All Systems Red.

I'm a fan of John Scalzi's work, and this Martha Wells novel felt a lot like "Fuzzy Nation" in it's setting, and a bit of Old Man's War in it's content (those reference are both Scalzi books in case that wasn't clear). I consider Scalzi a top tier sci-fi author, not in the "Great Ideas" authorship but in the "Enjoyable to Read" authorship, so when I say All Systems Red reminded me of Scalzi books that is a deep complement.

My main critique of the book is when I reflected on it I felt like... nothing really happened. Some researchers or something were on a new planet, they were sabotaged, they triumphed over the saboteurs, the murderbot was the narrator. It was good, but it was a very short story.

That said, I am excited to read the next one, so it's not a deal-breaker critique.

entry.title: The Ghost Brigades
entry.content:
I love Scalzi and this series continues to be really fun.

As I have mentioned before (maybe?) his work is consistently pulpy, interesting, and completely unconcerned about the science. It's not exactly magic, but it's more "Hey this would be a cool idea -- beam me up Scotty!" and less "Given our present understanding of physics this could be possible with these exact steps over the next 200 years". I love that. For me, fun sci-fi is about exploring fun ideas without worrying about what we have or think we might have today.

Ghost Brigades also goes into some interesting social dynamics between the Ghosts, basically child soldiers in adult bodies. It also gets into identity with the main character kind of being a soft fork of the antagonist. Really interesting and I'm excited to read the other... 5 books in this series!

entry.title: Old Goriot
entry.content:
I listened to the old goriot book on the recommendation of Man Carrying Thing (get used to me mentioning him, he's my new book guy man). In discussing Old Goriot, MCT mentioned that it was an interesting read because it is a fairly old novel but reads very modern, which was an interesting hook and both got me to read the thing and framed my reading quite a bit.

The book does in fact feel very modern. The story is about an old man (Goriot) living in what I can only describe as a long-term stay bed and breakfast in Paris. The majority of the other patrons are medical students, and they often have discussions during communal meals. Goriot lives for his daughters, giving everything he has to them to ensure their success in life, to the point where it kind of saps all of his energy and kills him -- but that's exactly how he wants to die so it's kind of a happy ending in a weird way.

One of my favorite parts of the book is when a character is describing building a diorama for school and everybody starts adding "-rama" to everything; think "This is a wonderful dinner-rama", "I'm enjoying this conversation-o-rama", "I'm going to sleep-o-rama". It's done to death when it's initially brought up and then there are callbacks throughout the rest of the book, the joke looping around from funny to too much back to funny by the end.

What I enjoy most about the book is just like Man Carrying Thing said, it feels modern, but in a unique way: it feels like a period piece, but more authenticity because it is written in the period it's set it. I'll try to explain...

Some details of daily life are never written down, at least not in a way a reader in the future would be able to make use of. For example we might know the big important things like royal family structure, but we don't know what peasants ate breakfast, when they ate breakfast, or even if they ate breakfast. I think about bi-phasic sleep, which was apparently the norm until artificial light became the norm. People slept for two 4 hour blocks and this was so common nobody thought to spell it out, at least not enough for it to be common knowledge today even though we do know many things about time periods where that was the norm -- like royal family structures.

Period pieces written today have an inherent distance between the characters and the author/reader; we weren't there so some details are either skipped over or fabricated entirely. We don't exactly know, or the author doesn't know, how much a coffee cost in 1810 Paris so they just kinda make up a believable number and everybody doesn't really care because it doesn't really matter. But it kinda does matter, even if we don't know what it cost, enough of those made up facts add up to a vibe that this world is fake and made up even if it was trying to be a real, grounded, period piece.

Old Goriot is not made up. People talk about money and social class expectations and random details about the world and I can only believe it is real because if I wrote a story about dating in 2025 and the characters were eating a meal in a McMinimins I would 100% go to a McMinimins and read the menu and name drop the exact order and price so everybody venmo's the main characters because that's authentic and easy goddammit.

So that's my main takeaway: reading Old Goriot feels more grounded than any period piece I've ever read (all 5 of them) because it's about [fairly] normal people talking about [fairly] normal things and it all feels real.

It is the most anthropologically interesting piece of fiction I have ever read.

Also the voice actor is great, he goes hard.

entry.title: Still Lost: Tales From 2080
entry.content:
Still Lost is a collection of short stories written by Sam A' Miller, better known as Sam O' Nella on YouTube. I've followed Sam for many years and enjoyed his funny infotainment. He hasn't been very active recently but randomly came out with a self punished book on Amazon and my current policy is that if a creator I like does a new and interesting thing that's outside their wheelhouse, I should give it a shot.

The stories take place in a near future sci-fi world in which aliens have invaded Earth and essentially turned it into a galactic nature preserve. That said the stories don't all directly connect to that theme and range from sci-fi allegories for drug use to making fun of academics.

Over all I like the quality of these stories. I thought they were fun and pulpy and frankly I think they could have been published by one of the indie sci-fi publishers -- I'm not sure why this was self published but I hope Miller keeps writing.

entry.title: Orange World and Other Stories (Karen Russell, 2019)
entry.content:
Orange World is a series of... mystical realism(?) short stories.

I listened to the audio-book of Orange World and thought it was exceptional. The voice actors for each story played their characters very well, enhancing the experience.

A few stories I enjoyed:

  • Bog Girl, about a boy's first love in a world where people are way too ok with necrophilia.
  • A story about a tornado rustler raising his last storm.
  • A woman in post-flood south-eastern USA who can echo-locate like a bat.
  • A demon blackmailing a new mother into giving it breast milk like a little freak.

I haven't read much of her work, but based on this I'd say Karen Russell is a great author. I'm excited to read more of her stuff.

entry.title: Strange Pictures (Uketsu, 2022)
entry.content:
I don't read much psycological horror/thriller but this was a gift and I figured why not.

What I liked about this was the feeling of putting the pieces together yourself between stories to connect the dots. It made me feel like a real detective! Even if it was definitely feeding you that narrative...

entry.title: Priestdaddy (2017)
entry.content:
I read Priestdaddy (Patricia Lockwood, 2017) because Jacob Geller, a really good games critic and essayist I follow, has suggested it at least four times in different mediums (Videos, Podcasts, Bluesky). It got to the point where I had to admit "Yeah this dude that I respect really likes this book, I guess I should read it." So I did. Like Geller I think you should read this book. It is beautiful, interesting, informational, and heartwarming.

Priestdaddy is so good. It's an autobiography written by a poet so even throw-away lines describing a van are the most vivid descriptions I've ever encountered. Every word is plucked from the aether and perfectly fit with the ones before and after creating a beautiful mosaic beautiful in the small and in the large, like a fractal. As you can probably tell it also inspired me to like... try writing more interesting pros.

It also taught me a lot about Catholicism. Not in the way a documentary teaches you about something, but in the way your childhood friend does; in bouts of lore dump and then long periods of subtle hints and vibes. For example Lockwood will explicitly tell you the structure of the church hierarchy, who reports to who and how they get there, but then spend the latter half of a chapter alluding but never going out and saying that a priest is a predator. It feels like I am conversational in a language but only have ~100 words in my vocabulary; I have the accent and the vibe and the important details but am immediately out of my depth five sentences in.

I should point out this book is not pro-catholic. I wouldn't say it's quite anti-catholic either, but it certainly wants to paint a complete picture of the church and like... a complete picture of the modern catholic churn doesn't exactly look good.
